name: Abdominal etching (high-definition lipo)

angle.text: Users who are lean but lack visible abs choose it to sculpt the lines of the abdominal muscles, so a six-pack shows without further fat loss. The visible change is the result itself; evidence comes from surgeon case series and one systematic review rather than randomized trials.

summary: Superficial liposuction that carves in the lines of the abs; documented in surgeon series and one systematic review, no randomized trials.
note: Superficial-plane liposuction; contour irregularities reported.
currentQuick:
Abdominal etching uses liposuction to remove fat in specific patterns so the abdominal muscle lines show more clearly. It was first described in 1993 and later extended to high-definition liposculpture with ultrasound-assisted devices.
It is mostly sought by lean, muscular people. Evidence consists of surgeon case series and one systematic review.
How it works: Fat is suctioned at variable depths, including superficial layers, along muscle landmarks such as the linea alba and tendinous intersections. Some versions add fat transfer into the muscle area.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include contour irregularities, asymmetry, umbilical changes, infection and bleeding, plus the general risks of liposuction.
deepLead:
Abdominal etching is a liposuction technique that removes fat at variable depths and in superficial layers to emphasize the lines of the abdominal muscles, giving the appearance of a defined abdomen or 'six-pack'. It was first described in the early 1990s and was later extended into high-definition liposculpture using VASER ultrasound technology.
It is sought mainly by people with a lean body and developed musculature who report not achieving the look through diet and exercise alone. Reviews describe published outcomes mostly as surgeon case series, and complications and patient selection have been discussed in the literature.

name: Lymph-sparing liposuction

angle.text: It is a liposuction method developed for lipedema, where excess leg fat is removed while protecting lymphatics, so the main use is medical rather than cosmetic. Appearance-minded readers see it as a way to slim the legs; reported outcomes are positive but from limited studies.

summary: Liposuction technique intended to protect lymph vessels, used mainly for lipedema rather than aesthetics; evidence reported as positive but limited.
note: Primarily a medical procedure for lipedema; insurance coverage varies.
currentQuick:
Lymph-sparing liposuction is liposuction designed to avoid damaging lymphatic vessels, used mainly to treat lipedema, a condition of painful symmetrical fat in the legs.
It is a medical rather than cosmetic procedure. Sources report positive results but the evidence base is small.
How it works: Surgeons use techniques such as tumescent or water-assisted liposuction with careful, slower fat removal intended to spare lymph vessels.
Risks and caveats: Surgery can damage lymphatic vessels, and vascular assessment is recommended beforehand. Multiple procedures are often needed, and insurance coverage varies.
deepLead:
Lymph-sparing liposuction is a form of liposuction designed for lipedema, a chronic condition of symmetrical fat accumulation, mainly in the legs of women. Its technique is intended to protect lymphatic vessels during fat removal.
It is primarily a medical rather than cosmetic procedure. Studies cited by Wikipedia report positive short- and long-term results, with the highest-quality evidence coming from tumescent liposuction, though multiple procedures are often needed.

name: CoolSculpting Elite

chain: Fat cells die off over weeks
angle.text: People use fat freezing to shrink stubborn pockets such as the belly or flanks and sharpen body contour without surgery. Studies document modest local fat reduction over a few weeks; a rare paradoxical fat-growth complication is also documented.

summary: Allergan's fat-freezing system; modest, documented fat reduction with a rare paradoxical fat-growth complication.
note: Paradoxical adipose hyperplasia reported in about 0.12 to 1 percent of cases.
currentQuick:
CoolSculpting Elite is Allergan's newer fat-freezing system. It cools targeted fat through the skin to reduce small areas such as the chin, abdomen and thighs without surgery.
Reviews report modest reductions in fat thickness and high satisfaction, though data quality is described as low.
How it works: Controlled cooling of subcutaneous fat (cryolipolysis) is applied through applicators on the skin over the target area.
Risks and caveats: Redness, numbness, swelling and bruising are common and usually resolve in weeks. A rare complication, paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, enlarges treated fat and may need surgery.
deepLead:
CoolSculpting Elite is a version of the CoolSculpting cryolipolysis system, a non-invasive procedure that reduces localized subcutaneous fat by controlled cooling. It is made by Allergan Aesthetics, which acquired the CoolSculpting brand from Zeltiq in 2017.
The FDA has cleared cryolipolysis for areas including the chin, jawline, arms, flanks, abdomen, thighs and under the buttocks. Reviews report modest fat reductions with high satisfaction, and a rare complication called paradoxical adipose hyperplasia has been described.

name: CoolTone

angle.text: It is discussed as an add-on to fat freezing, with the idea that magnetic contractions tone the area so the result looks firmer and more defined. The tone claim rests on manufacturer marketing; almost no published evidence exists for the device itself.

summary: A magnetic muscle-stimulation add-on to fat freezing, with almost no published evidence of its own.
note: Only one small registered trial found, with no results.
currentQuick:
CoolTone is a device that uses magnetic fields to make muscles contract, marketed for toning areas such as the lower buttock. It is discussed alongside fat-freezing treatments.
The only human study found is a 15-person registered trial, with no results available.
How it works: Magnetic muscle stimulation induces muscle contractions in the treated area; the intent is increased tone. No mechanistic study specific to CoolTone was found.
Risks and caveats: No CoolTone-specific safety data were found. The related fat-freezing procedure has reported side effects including redness, numbness, bruising and, rarely, paradoxical adipose hyperplasia.
deepLead:
CoolTone is a magnetic muscle-stimulation device marketed for body contouring, and it is discussed in appearance circles as an add-on to fat-reduction treatments such as cryolipolysis ("fat freezing"), the technology behind CoolSculpting. Magnetic muscle stimulation uses a changing magnetic field to make targeted muscles contract, with the aim of increasing tone.
Published evidence located for this entry is minimal. The only record found is a small registered clinical trial, started in 2022 with 15 participants, that compares CoolSculpting combined with CoolTone against CoolSculpting alone for the "banana roll" area beneath the buttocks. Its status is listed as unknown and no results were found. Cryolipolysis itself has been studied more extensively, with a 2023 review of 18 studies reporting modest ultrasound-measured fat thickness reductions and low data quality.

name: Emsculpt Neo

chain: Forced muscle contractions plus RF heat
angle.text: Users take it to firm and slim areas like the abs, glutes, thighs and arms by combining muscle contractions with fat heating. Reviews report fat reduction and muscle gains, though many studies use the same device and often come from the maker's circle.

summary: A BTL machine that pairs electromagnetic muscle contractions with RF fat heating; reviews exist, but the studies largely use the same device.
note: Much of the published data uses the manufacturer's own device.
currentQuick:
Emsculpt Neo is a non-invasive contouring device that combines strong magnetic muscle contractions with radiofrequency heating of fat. It is marketed for toning and fat reduction on the abdomen, buttocks, thighs and arms.
Systematic reviews exist, though they describe small imaging-based studies, and the combination-device studies in one review all used the same device.
How it works: Alternating magnetic fields stimulate motor nerves to produce contractions stronger than voluntary exercise, while RF energy heats subcutaneous fat.
Risks and caveats: Reviews assessed safety alongside efficacy. The device is FDA-cleared for several body-contouring indications according to manufacturer-derived information; no long-term comparative data were located.
deepLead:
Emsculpt Neo is a non-invasive body-contouring device made by BTL Industries that combines high-intensity focused electromagnetic (HIFEM) energy, which causes strong muscle contractions, with radiofrequency (RF) heating of fat. It is marketed for increasing muscle tone and reducing fat in areas such as the abdomen, buttocks, thighs and arms.
Systematic reviews published in 2023 to 2025 have examined the electromagnetic body-contouring literature and the HIFEM-plus-RF combination specifically. Much of the research was manufacturer-linked device studies measured by imaging and photographs, and one review notes that all studies in its scope used the BTL device.

name: Emface

chain: RF heats skin, stimulates facial muscles
angle.text: It is promoted as a needle-free way to smooth wrinkles and lift the face over a short course of sessions. The headline improvement figures come mainly from manufacturer-supported studies.

summary: A needle-free RF plus facial-muscle-stimulation treatment whose headline numbers come from the manufacturer.
note: No independent trials were found.
currentQuick:
Emface combines radiofrequency heating of the skin with electrical stimulation of facial muscles. It is marketed for wrinkles, muscle tone and a lifted look.
The quoted results come from manufacturer-linked data; no independent trials were found.
How it works: RF energy heats the dermis to stimulate collagen remodeling, while stimulation induces facial muscle contractions.
Risks and caveats: No Emface-specific safety data were found. A 2025 study of non-surgical aesthetic treatments generally reports that complications are underreported.
deepLead:
Emface is a facial treatment from BTL Aesthetics that applies radiofrequency (RF) energy to the skin together with high-intensity facial electrical stimulation (HIFES) of facial muscles, marketed for wrinkle reduction, muscle tone and a lifting effect without needles. It is typically described as a four-session course of about 20 minutes each.
The figures commonly quoted for it, such as 37% wrinkle improvement, come from manufacturer-linked data repeated in an AI-generated encyclopedia entry. No independent peer-reviewed trial of Emface was found among the sources for this article.

name: truSculpt iD

angle.text: Users consider it for non-invasive slimming of localized fat on areas such as the abdomen. Many small trials are registered, but few published results are available for this specific device.

summary: A Cutera radiofrequency fat-reduction device with many small registered trials but few published results.
note: Outcome data for the specific device were not retrieved.
currentQuick:
truSculpt iD is a non-invasive radiofrequency device marketed for reducing localized fat. It sits alongside freezing, laser and ultrasound approaches.
Several small registered trials exist, plus published studies of related monopolar RF devices.
How it works: Radiofrequency energy heats fat tissue while the skin is kept cooler, with the aim of reducing fat thickness.
Risks and caveats: No device-specific safety data were retrieved.
deepLead:
truSculpt iD is a non-invasive radiofrequency (RF) body-contouring device from Cutera for localized fat reduction, with related truSculpt devices registered in trials since 2009. Radiofrequency is one of several energy modalities used for non-invasive fat reduction, alongside cryotherapy, ultrasound and laser.
Published evidence includes a 2020 ultrasound study of a temperature-controlled multi-frequency monopolar RF device on the abdomen and flanks, a 2017 study of 1-MHz monopolar RF for lower facial fat, and a series of registered truSculpt trials of 4 to 70 participants.

name: Cavitation (ultrasonic fat)

angle.text: Forum users, especially for DIY face slimming, use cavitation devices hoping to spot-reduce fat in the cheeks and jaw area. Only small registered trials exist and no cosmetic results were located for the home-use claim.

summary: Low-frequency ultrasound devices marketed to burst fat cells; popular for DIY face-slimming, with only small registered trials and no cosmetic results found.
note: Home devices are untested for facial fat reduction in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Ultrasonic cavitation uses low-frequency ultrasound through a handheld probe to try to disrupt fat under the skin without surgery. It is sold in clinics and as cheap home units, and some looksmaxxing posters use it for the face and chin.
Forum opinion is split between users reporting benefit and users reporting none. A few small human trials are registered, mainly on abdominal fat in women, with no results summarised in the registry entries.
How it works: The physics idea is that ultrasound creates bubbles that collapse near cells and damage membranes; this is documented in lab studies of cells and vessels. Whether commercial devices do this in living fat enough to change appearance has not been shown in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed do not report adverse events from cosmetic cavitation. Lab studies show cavitation can damage cells and small vessels, and device quality varies widely. Regulatory status varies by device and country and is not covered by the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Ultrasonic cavitation, also sold as "lipocavitation", is a non-invasive body-contouring treatment in which a handheld device applies low-frequency ultrasound to the skin over a fat deposit. Marketing and forum guides say the sound waves form tiny bubbles in the tissue that burst and break open fat cells, after which the body clears the contents.
Cavitation itself, the formation and collapse of gas bubbles in a liquid under ultrasound, is a well-studied physical phenomenon, and laboratory work has examined how inertial cavitation affects cells and blood vessels in vitro. Whether consumer or spa devices reproduce these effects in living subcutaneous fat at a cosmetically visible scale is a separate question; the sources reviewed here include a handful of small registered clinical trials, mostly of abdominal fat in women, with no published results summarised in the registry entries.
In looksmaxxing communities the treatment is discussed mainly as an at-home method for "spot reducing" facial and submental fat using inexpensive devices. Some users report improvements; others describe it as ineffective.

name: Endermologie / LPG

angle.text: It is used to soften the look of cellulite and improve body contour through machine massage. Small studies report contour and texture changes; large controlled evidence is limited.

summary: A French roll-and-suction massage machine for cellulite and contour; small studies exist, large controlled evidence is thin.
note: Evidence is from small, short studies.
currentQuick:
Endermologie is a motorised roller-and-suction massage treatment developed in France and sold for cellulite and body contouring. It is typically studied as a course of about fifteen sessions over several weeks.
Small studies of tens to a hundred or so women report on cellulite grade and measurements, and it is also used for lymphedema alongside compression.
How it works: The device pulls and rolls the skin and the tissue beneath it with suction and rollers, a mechanical massage of subcutaneous tissue.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed describe it as FDA-approved as a massage system and do not detail adverse events in the abstracts available. Larger controlled studies were not found among them.
deepLead:
Endermologie, produced by the French company LPG, is a machine-assisted massage system that rolls the skin between motorised rollers while applying suction, intended to improve the look of cellulite and body contour. It was originally developed in the late 1970s in France to soften scars and standardise physical therapy, and clinicians then noticed changes in contour and skin texture in treated patients.
Small clinical studies have evaluated it. One study of 33 women with cellulite gave 15 sessions twice weekly, and another of 118 women used a similar schedule; both assessed cellulite grade and body measurements. These papers describe the device as FDA-approved as a massage system, and the 2009 authors described it as lacking clinical study at that point.
It has also been explored for lymphedema in combination with compression bandaging, a medical rather than cosmetic use.

name: Qwo (collagenase)

angle.text: It is an injectable approved for cellulite dimples on women's buttocks, aimed at a smoother look of the area. Clinical trials studied dimple improvement, with bruising the main studied concern.

summary: A clinician-injected collagenase approved for buttock cellulite in women; bruising is a main concern and bruising is the main studied concern.
note: Prescription procedure; bruising is a studied effect.
currentQuick:
Qwo is an enzyme injection given by clinicians to treat dimpling from cellulite on the buttocks of adult women. It uses a collagenase from bacteria to break the fibrous bands under the skin.
A large Phase 3 study is registered, and later studies focus on reducing bruising.
How it works: The enzymes cut collagen in the fibrous septae that tether skin and form dimples, and mostly stay at the injection site.
Risks and caveats: Bruising is a prominent effect, and the parent collagenase product lists pain, swelling, itching and rare allergic reactions. It is prescription-only and administered in clinics.
deepLead:
Qwo (collagenase clostridium histolyticum-aaes, or CCH-aaes) is an injectable enzyme treatment for cellulite, made by Endo Aesthetics, approved as a subcutaneous injection for moderate to severe cellulite on the buttocks of adult women. The enzymes are intended to disrupt the fibrous septae that give rise to cellulite dimples.
It is a brand of the same bacterial collagenase family that Endo markets as Xiaflex for Dupuytren contracture and Peyronie disease; Wikipedia lists Qwo among the trade names but does not describe it separately.
In clinical practice reports, physicians have also used it off-label on thighs and diluted beyond the proprietary diluent. A Phase 3 long-term study of 483 patients and several Phase 4 and 2 studies on reducing bruising are registered.

name: Ultrasound skin tightening

angle.text: People use microfocused ultrasound such as Ulthera to lift sagging skin on the jawline, neck and brows without surgery. Published cohort studies exist for face and neck; detailed effect sizes were not verified here.

summary: Heat from focused ultrasound aimed beneath the skin to tighten the face and neck; published cohort studies exist but detailed effect sizes were not verified.
note: Clinician-performed; results differ across studies.
currentQuick:
Microfocused ultrasound treatments send focused ultrasound energy under the skin to heat deeper layers and tighten sagging areas such as the brow, jawline and neck.
Published cohort studies report on facial and neck laxity, and several trials are registered.
How it works: Focused ultrasound heats tissue at set depths below the surface while sparing the epidermis.
Risks and caveats: Studies describe the safety profile of nonablative tightening as good with limited efficacy in general; detailed adverse events were not in the abstracts available.
deepLead:
Ultrasound skin tightening uses intense focused ultrasound (IFUS), also called microfocused ultrasound, to deliver heat at specific depths beneath the skin while sparing the surface, with the aim of tightening and lifting sagging tissue without surgery. Branded systems such as Ulthera are used in registered trials on the face, neck and arms.
Published clinical studies include a rater-blinded prospective cohort study of the face and neck with brow lift as the main target, a single-treatment study in 22 Korean patients with blinded clinician assessment, a multiple-pass study of the lower face and neck, and a study of infraorbital laxity. The introductions of these papers describe the technique as having excellent safety but limited efficacy in the case of nonablative tightening generally.
A 2025 paper examined a high-intensity parallel ultrasound variant.

name: Microneedling (SkinPen)

angle.text: It is used for acne scars, wrinkles and overall texture, sometimes combined with platelet-rich plasma. Several small trials on scars, wrinkles and acne are registered for SkinPen; published results were not located here.

summary: Branded electric microneedling pen with several small registered trials on scars, wrinkles and acne; published results were not located here.
note: Infection risk with unsterile or non-clinical use.
currentQuick:
SkinPen is an electric microneedling device that makes controlled tiny punctures in the skin, used by clinicians for acne scars and signs of aging.
Several small trials are registered for different skin conditions.
How it works: Repeated tiny punctures are thought to trigger skin repair and collagen production; this is the standard description of microneedling.
Risks and caveats: Infection is a documented risk in untrained or non-sterile settings, including a 2024 CDC report tied to a spa facial procedure.
deepLead:
Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy, skin needling or dermarolling, is a cosmetic procedure in which tiny sterile needles repeatedly puncture the skin; SkinPen is a branded electric microneedling device used in registered clinical trials. It has been used for scarring and acne, and is combined in some practices with platelet-rich plasma.
Registered SkinPen trials cover wrinkles of the neck, acne scars on the face and back, acne vulgaris, hand aging and vitiligo. No results from these registrations are summarised in the sources reviewed here.
The sources reviewed do not describe the device history or its regulatory clearance, although it is commonly described as FDA-cleared.

name: Dermastamp

angle.text: Looksmax forum users stamp skin, under-eye lines and brows, sometimes alongside minoxidil, hoping for smoother skin and fuller brows. Microneedling generally has studies, but no cosmetic trials of the stamp itself were found.

summary: A handheld needle-stamp used for DIY microneedling of skin and brows; no cosmetic trials found for the stamp itself.
note: Infection risk with non-sterile use.
currentQuick:
A dermastamp is a small stamp-like microneedling tool used at home. Forum users apply it to brows, skin and fine lines.
No trials of the stamp itself for appearance were found.
How it works: It presses short needles into the skin to create tiny punctures, which microneedling proponents say triggers repair and improves topical absorption.
Risks and caveats: Infection is a recognised concern with non-sterile or untrained microneedling, per Wikipedia. Device quality and hygiene vary.
deepLead:
A dermastamp is a handheld microneedling tool that presses a pad of short needles into the skin in a stamping motion, as opposed to the rolling action of a dermaroller. It is discussed on looksmax.org for use on skin, brows, under-eye lines and as a way to help topicals penetrate.
Laboratory research on related oscillating microneedle devices has looked at improving delivery of drugs such as imiquimod through the skin in basal cell carcinoma. No published trials of dermastamps for appearance outcomes were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Jet peel (needle-free)

angle.text: Clinics offer it as a needle-free facial for hydration and a smoother look. Little has been published on it.

summary: Needle-free pressurised-jet facial for hydration and product delivery, with almost nothing published behind it.
note: Only a small registered pilot comparison exists; no results published.
currentQuick:
A jet peel uses a pressurised stream of fluid or gas to treat or deliver products to the skin without needles. It is offered in clinics as a hydration or glow treatment.
The only related research found is a small registered comparison against another hydrating treatment, with no published results.
How it works: A handheld device propels a fine jet of saline, oxygen or serum at the skin surface; providers say this exfoliates lightly and drives products in.
Risks and caveats: No safety data specific to jet peel were found in the sources reviewed. Needle-free devices are generally described as low-downtime, but this has not been established by published trials.
deepLead:
A jet peel is an aesthetic skin procedure in which a handheld device propels a fine, pressurised stream of fluid or gas (commonly saline, oxygen or a serum) at the skin surface without needles. Clinics market it for hydration, a smoother appearance and as a way to deliver topical products.
Published evidence is very sparse. The only relevant record found is a small registered comparison of a hydrating treatment and a jet peel for facial skin hydration (23 participants, listed as completed in 2026), for which no results are available. No peer-reviewed trial results on jet peel are summarised here.

name: Hydrafacial Keravive

angle.text: It is pitched as a salon scalp facial for scalp health and hair quality. The hair appearance claim is based on marketing; only registered studies exist, with no published results.

summary: Salon scalp facial from HydraFacial pitched for scalp health and hair quality; only registered studies, no published results.
note: Registered studies have no published results.
currentQuick:
Keravive is a clinic scalp treatment that cleanses, exfoliates and applies serums to the scalp. It is marketed for scalp health and hair quality, including for thinning hair.
Two small studies are registered, one completed in androgenetic alopecia, but no results were found.
How it works: A handheld device performs cleansing and exfoliation and delivers topical products to the scalp, in the manner of the brand's facial treatment.
Risks and caveats: No safety data were found in the sources reviewed. Whether it affects hair growth has not been shown by published trials.
deepLead:
Hydrafacial Keravive (also marketed as HydraScalp) is a scalp treatment from the HydraFacial brand that adapts the company's multi-step facial platform for the scalp, aimed at cleansing, exfoliation and the delivery of topical serums to improve scalp health and hair appearance.
Evidence is limited to registered studies. A 44-person study of the treatment in androgenetic alopecia is listed as completed, and a 15-person study pairing a scalp serum with the treatment in people with self-perceived hair thinning is registered but not yet recruiting. No published results were found.

name: Oxygen facial

angle.text: People get it before events for immediate hydration and a glow with no downtime. Serum ingredients like hyaluronic acid are studied on their own; no trials of the oxygen treatment itself exist.

summary: Pressurised-oxygen facial that infuses serums for an instant glow; no trials of the cosmetic treatment exist.
note: Visible effects are attributed by cited sources mainly to the serums; sourcing is thin.
currentQuick:
An oxygen facial blows purified oxygen across the skin while applying serums such as hyaluronic acid. Spas offer it for instant hydration and glow without downtime.
No clinical trials of the cosmetic treatment were found; the one encyclopedia source says evidence for the oxygen itself is limited.
How it works: A wand delivers a pressurised oxygen stream that is claimed to help serums absorb and support skin; this is not strongly supported scientifically according to the source.
Risks and caveats: No adverse-event data were found. It is described as non-invasive with no downtime, and is distinct from medical hyperbaric oxygen therapy.
deepLead:
An oxygen facial is a cosmetic skincare treatment in which a handheld wand directs a stream of pressurised, purified oxygen onto the skin together with serums, typically containing hyaluronic acid, vitamins and antioxidants. It is offered for immediate hydration, a plumper look and a "glow", with no downtime.
Grokipedia states that scientific support for the oxygen itself is limited and that dermatologists attribute visible improvements mainly to the serums. No clinical trials of cosmetic oxygen facials were found; the oxygen-related trials that turn up in searches concern medical oxygen therapy.

name: LED light facial

angle.text: It is used in clinics and at home for acne and skin ageing, with blue light aimed at acne and red/near-infrared at texture. Small trials show preliminary results.

summary: Coloured-light facial for acne and skin ageing, with small trials and preliminary evidence.
note: Evidence is preliminary; many registered trials lack results.
currentQuick:
LED facials shine specific wavelengths of light on the skin, with blue used for acne and red or near-infrared for ageing. They are offered in clinics and as home masks.
Small studies and registrations exist, and Wikipedia describes the evidence as preliminary.
How it works: Light is thought to be absorbed by mitochondria in skin cells, influencing repair and inflammation (photobiomodulation).
Risks and caveats: Side effects are described as rare and mild, such as itching or redness. Photodynamic therapy, which adds a light-sensitising drug, carries more risks and is a separate procedure.
deepLead:
An LED light facial is a clinic or at-home treatment that exposes the face to light-emitting diodes at selected wavelengths (blue, red, near-infrared and others), usually for acne, skin ageing and general skin quality. It belongs to the family of low-level light therapy, or photobiomodulation.
Wikipedia describes the proposed mechanism as light interacting with mitochondria, and describes the therapy as having rare, mild side effects, while noting that its own evidence base is flagged as needing stronger sourcing. Small trials of LED treatment for facial rejuvenation exist; results for most registered studies are not available.

name: Dermalinfusion

angle.text: It is used to exfoliate and infuse serums, notably for dark marks in skin of color. The evidence found is a single small 2014 study on post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

summary: Branded exfoliate-and-infuse facial with one small published study on hyperpigmentation.
note: Sources are very thin.
currentQuick:
Dermalinfusion pairs skin exfoliation with serum infusion in one pass. It is offered as a facial treatment.
The only publication found examined it alongside a peptide for dark marks after inflammation in darker skin.
How it works: A handheld tip is described as exfoliating while delivering a serum to the skin.
Risks and caveats: No safety information was available in the sources reviewed.
deepLead: Dermalinfusion is a branded aesthetic procedure that combines a form of exfoliation with simultaneous serum infusion through a handheld tip. Evidence found is limited to one 2014 Journal of Drugs in Dermatology study that combined topical delivery with dermalinfusion of decapeptide-12 to treat post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in skin of color.

name: Jessner peel

chain: Acid mix sheds top skin layer
angle.text: It is a superficial peel used for fine lines, acne marks and uneven pigment, and to prime skin before deeper TCA or retinoic peels. Evidence specific to Jessner's solution is limited.

summary: A superficial resorcinol-salicylic-lactic acid peel, also used to prime skin before TCA; evidence specific to it is thin.
note: Specific trial data are sparse; pigment complications are a recognised peel concern in darker skin.
currentQuick:
The Jessner peel is a light chemical peel made from resorcinol, salicylic acid and lactic acid. It is used for pigment, acne and texture concerns and sometimes as a first layer before a deeper TCA peel.
Research specific to it is limited to small comparative studies, for example in melasma.
How it works: The acids cause controlled superficial injury, after which the outer skin layers shed and renew.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects of peels include stinging, redness, dryness, photosensitivity and, less often, pigment change or scarring.
deepLead:
The Jessner peel is a superficial chemical peel based on Jessner's solution, a mixture of resorcinol, salicylic acid and lactic acid. Chemical peels are procedures in which an acid or other agent is applied to the skin to cause controlled injury, after which the skin sheds and renews itself; the general category is described as being used for fine lines, acne scarring and uneven pigmentation. Retinoic acid peels are described as commonly being preceded by a Jessner peel.
In dermatology literature the Jessner solution is also used as a pre-treatment step before a medium-depth trichloroacetic acid (TCA) peel, a combination known as the Jessner's + TCA peel. Authors of a 2017 paper on TCA technique noted that physicians often choose lighter peels, such as glycolic acid or Jessner peels, and various lasers for patients with darker skin out of concern about pigmentary complications from deeper peels.
Published human research specific to the Jessner peel is limited. A 2021 comparative study in Indian women with melasma compared a 35% glycolic acid peel with a Jessner peel as add-ons to a triple topical combination.

name: TCA peel

chain: Fewer scars, even tone, fewer lines
angle.text: It is a medium-depth clinic peel used for scars, pigment and sun damage. Decades of small clinical studies cover these uses.

summary: A medium-depth acid peel with decades of small clinical studies for scars, pigment and photoaging, and a real burn and scarring risk when done wrongly.
note: FDA warned in 2024 against certain TCA peel products used without professional supervision.
currentQuick:
A TCA peel applies trichloroacetic acid to the face to cause controlled injury, so damaged outer skin sheds and new skin forms. It is used for photoaging, acne scars and pigment.
Studies are mostly small, but the technique has been described in the literature since the 1980s.
How it works: TCA coagulates skin proteins in the epidermis and upper dermis, followed by shedding and collagen remodelling.
Risks and caveats: Redness, crusting, pigment change and scarring are documented; the FDA issued a warning in 2024 about unsupervised use of certain products.
deepLead:
A TCA peel is a chemical peel using trichloroacetic acid, generally classed as medium depth and performed in a clinic or surgical setting by a medical provider. The acid coagulates skin proteins, causing controlled necrosis of the epidermis and upper dermis, followed by shedding and collagen remodelling.
TCA at roughly 10 to 50 percent is used for resurfacing in acne scars, fine wrinkles and photoaging, while stronger concentrations are used on individual lesions such as warts. German dermatologist Paul Unna reported its use in peels in 1882.
The published literature includes many small clinical studies and technique papers, covering photoaging, melasma, atrophic acne scars and pigmented lesions. In July 2024 the US FDA warned against using certain TCA peel products without professional supervision because of burn and scarring risks.
